title: The Ratio Nobody Regulates
endLine: Hematocrit is a ratio; the kidney regulates its numerator by local oxygen.

scenes.tts: Two tubes of spun blood. An endurance athlete can show the shorter red layer and still carry more red cells than an untrained friend. How does one number fall while the cells rise?
scenes.narration: Two tubes of spun blood. An endurance athlete can show the shorter red layer and still carry more red cells than an untrained friend. How does one number fall while the cells rise?
scenes.caption: Two tubes of spun blood. An endurance athlete can show the shorter red layer and still carry more red cells than an untrained friend. How does one number fall while the cells rise?
scenes.visual: THE WORLD, built here and kept for the whole film (16:9). COLOUR BY CONCEPT, same in every scene: red cells RED; plasma AMBER; oxygen CYAN; erythropoietin MAGENTA; kidney tissue SLATE outlines; marrow a pale TAN block. A small 'schematic' tag sits at bottom right all film. LAYOUT: LEFT 35% holds a tall spun-blood tube on a vertical scale marked 0 to 60 percent, its lower part a packed RED column, the upper part AMBER plasma, with a WHITE marker and read-out at the top of the red column. RIGHT 65% holds a horizontal vessel band across the middle, pale with RED cells drifting left to right; above it a pale TAN marrow block with a short opening onto the vessel; below it a SLATE patch of kidney tissue showing three tubule outlines with two round interstitial cells sitting between them, each carrying a small CYAN oxygen gauge. HOOK MOTION: open on TWO tubes side by side in the left panel, labelled 'untrained' and 'trained'; both are the same total height, the trained one's RED column visibly shorter. Beside each tube a small stack of RED dots builds, one dot at a time, and the trained stack grows TALLER than the untrained one while its red column stays shorter. On the question, white text across the top: 'Fewer? Or more?' Then the trained tube and both dot stacks slide out of frame and the single untrained tube stays for the rest of the film. Red cells keep drifting along the vessel band throughout.

Title 'The Ratio Nobody Regulates' fades in over the top of the frame for 2 s while the question text fades out beneath it. The single tube settles, its RED column rising smoothly to its resting height; red cells keep drifting along the vessel band and the CYAN kidney gauges glow steadily.

scenes.tts: Hematocrit is a ratio: the volume of packed red cells over the volume of whole blood. Take made-up round numbers for an untrained adult. Two point two litres of red cells, two point eight litres of plasma. Forty-four percent.
scenes.narration: Hematocrit is a ratio: the volume of packed red cells over the volume of whole blood. Take made-up round numbers for an untrained adult. 2.2 L of red cells, 2.8 L of plasma. 44 percent.
scenes.caption: Hematocrit is a ratio: the volume of packed red cells over the volume of whole blood. Take made-up round numbers for an untrained adult. 2.2 L of red cells, 2.8 L of plasma. 44 percent.
scenes.visual: Push in on the tube until it fills about 70% of frame height; the vessel, marrow and kidney patch stay visible, smaller, at the right. The tube divides into labelled parts as the words arrive: the RED column gets the label '2.2 L red cells', the AMBER column the label '2.8 L plasma', and a WHITE bracket spans both, labelled '5.0 L blood'. A tag 'teaching numbers' appears under the tube and stays all film. On 'forty-four percent', the two volumes slide into a large fraction beside the tube, '2.2 / 5.0', which resolves into '44%' at size 34, and the WHITE marker on the scale snaps to 44. Red cells keep drifting in the vessel band.

scenes.tts: A ratio answers to its top and its bottom separately. Add red cells and it rises. Add plasma and it falls. And nothing in the body regulates the ratio itself.
scenes.narration: A ratio answers to its top and its bottom separately. Add red cells and it rises. Add plasma and it falls. And nothing in the body regulates the ratio itself.
scenes.caption: A ratio answers to its top and its bottom separately. Add red cells and it rises. Add plasma and it falls. And nothing in the body regulates the ratio itself.
scenes.visual: The fraction '2.2 / 5.0 = 44%' stays beside the tube and both of its terms stay live: the numerator tracks the RED column, the denominator the whole bracket. On 'add red cells', the RED column grows while the AMBER stays put, the marker climbs above 44, and the numerator counts up with it. The tube rewinds to 44. On 'add plasma', the AMBER column grows while the RED stays put, the marker sinks below 44, and the denominator counts up. The tube rewinds to 44 again. On the last sentence, a small WHITE dial labelled 'set the ratio?' appears beside the marker, is struck through once and fades out; the numerator and denominator labels pulse instead.

scenes.tts: Pregnancy expands plasma more than red cells, so hematocrit falls. In the first days at altitude it runs the other way. A diuresis shrinks plasma, and hematocrit rises before red cell mass has changed much.
scenes.narration: Pregnancy expands plasma more than red cells, so hematocrit falls. In the first days at altitude it runs the other way. A diuresis shrinks plasma, and hematocrit rises before red cell mass has changed much.
scenes.caption: Pregnancy expands plasma more than red cells, so hematocrit falls. In the first days at altitude it runs the other way. A diuresis shrinks plasma, and hematocrit rises before red cell mass has changed much.
scenes.visual: The tube keeps its place and changes twice, each change a transformation of the same two columns, with a ghost outline of the starting 44 level left on the scale for comparison. First the label above the tube reads 'pregnancy': the AMBER column grows a long step while the RED column grows a short step, and the WHITE marker slides DOWN below the ghost line. The label then morphs to 'altitude, first days': the AMBER column shrinks while the RED column holds exactly still, and the marker slides UP above the ghost line. A small AMBER drop icon leaves the tube on 'a diuresis'. On the last words, a short caption under the tube: 'red cell mass: little changed'. No numbers are put on either change.

scenes.tts: So a concentration cannot give you a mass. For that you need plasma volume by indicator dilution, or hemoglobin mass by carbon monoxide rebreathing. The spun tube reports a share, never a count.
scenes.narration: So a concentration cannot give you a mass. For that you need plasma volume by indicator dilution, or hemoglobin mass by carbon monoxide rebreathing. The spun tube reports a share, never a count.
scenes.caption: So a concentration cannot give you a mass. For that you need plasma volume by indicator dilution, or hemoglobin mass by carbon monoxide rebreathing. The spun tube reports a share, never a count.
scenes.visual: Pull back so the tube sits at the left and the vessel, marrow and kidney patch return to full size at the right. On 'cannot give you a mass', a question mark rises from the tube toward a faint grid of RED dots over the vessel band, then fades. Two labelled method cards slide in beside the tube, one at a time, each a plain icon: a syringe with a spreading AMBER tracer, 'indicator dilution', and a mask with a breath arrow, 'CO rebreathing'. Each card pulses once and then shrinks to a small chip at the left edge. On the last sentence, the WHITE marker on the tube is circled and labelled 'a share'; the grid of RED dots over the vessel is circled with a dashed line and labelled 'a count', and the two circles sit plainly apart.

scenes.tts: Here is the one idea. Nothing in the body regulates that ratio. The kidney regulates its numerator, the red cells, and it does that by reading the oxygen in its own patch of tissue.
scenes.narration: Here is the one idea. Nothing in the body regulates that ratio. The kidney regulates its numerator, the red cells, and it does that by reading the oxygen in its own patch of tissue.
scenes.caption: Here is the one idea. Nothing in the body regulates that ratio. The kidney regulates its numerator, the red cells, and it does that by reading the oxygen in its own patch of tissue.
scenes.visual: The whole world stays on screen and moving. On 'nothing in the body regulates that ratio', the WHITE marker and the '44%' read-out dim to half brightness. On 'regulates its numerator', the RED column and the numerator of the fraction brighten to full and a MAGENTA arrow draws itself from the kidney patch up to the marrow block and on into the vessel band, where a few new RED cells join the drift. On 'reading the oxygen in its own patch', the camera pushes a little toward the kidney patch: the two interstitial cells brighten and a CYAN halo appears around each, confined to the tissue immediately around them, so the halo plainly does not reach the vessel band or the tube. Label by the cells, 5 words or fewer: 'oxygen, here'.

scenes.tts: Those readers are fibroblast-like interstitial cells, sitting between the kidney tubules rather than in them. They lie in a relatively low-oxygen zone, so a small fall in blood oxygen content lowers their oxygen enough to matter.
scenes.narration: Those readers are fibroblast-like interstitial cells, sitting between the kidney tubules rather than in them. They lie in a relatively low-oxygen zone, so a small fall in blood oxygen content lowers their oxygen enough to matter.
scenes.caption: Those readers are fibroblast-like interstitial cells, sitting between the kidney tubules rather than in them. They lie in a relatively low-oxygen zone, so a small fall in blood oxygen content lowers their oxygen enough to matter.
scenes.visual: Push in until the kidney patch fills about 65% of frame height; the tube and vessel band stay at the edges of frame. The three SLATE tubule outlines are now large and open, and the two star-shaped interstitial cells sit clearly BETWEEN them, not inside them, each labelled once: 'interstitial cell'. A dashed outline briefly offers the inside of a tubule and is struck through. On 'relatively low-oxygen zone', a CYAN background wash over this patch is visibly paler than a CYAN wash near the vessel band at the top of frame, with the label 'relatively low oxygen'. On the last clause, the RED cells in the vessel band thin out a little and each cell's CYAN oxygen gauge drops a short step; the gauges carry a small 'schematic' tag.

scenes.tts: The switch inside them is hypoxia-inducible factor two alpha. In a well-oxygenated cell, hydroxylase enzymes that need oxygen, iron and two-oxoglutarate mark it for destruction. When oxygen falls, it accumulates and turns on the erythropoietin gene.
scenes.narration: The switch inside them is HIF-2 alpha. In a well-oxygenated cell, hydroxylase enzymes that need oxygen, iron and 2-oxoglutarate mark it for destruction. When oxygen falls, it accumulates and turns on the erythropoietin gene.
scenes.caption: The switch inside them is HIF-2 alpha. In a well-oxygenated cell, hydroxylase enzymes that need oxygen, iron and 2-oxoglutarate mark it for destruction. When oxygen falls, it accumulates and turns on the erythropoietin gene.
scenes.visual: One interstitial cell swells to fill most of the frame; keep it a plain labelled-block cartoon, never a molecular structure. Inside it, MAGENTA blocks labelled 'HIF-2 alpha' drift in. A SLATE hexagon labelled 'hydroxylase' sits beside them with three small input chips feeding it, labelled 'oxygen', 'iron', '2-oxoglutarate'. In the first, well-oxygenated state (the CYAN wash bright), the hydroxylase stamps each arriving MAGENTA block with a small tag and the block is dragged off frame to a bin icon labelled 'destroyed'. On 'when oxygen falls', the CYAN wash dims, the 'oxygen' input chip empties, the hydroxylase greys out, and MAGENTA blocks now pile up and travel to a labelled box in the cell marked 'EPO gene', which lights up and releases MAGENTA dots out of the cell. At most 6 objects on screen.

scenes.tts: In lowlanders breathing thin air, plasma erythropoietin rises within the first day or two. The new red cells arrive later. Why does the cell count lag the hormone?
scenes.narration: In lowlanders breathing thin air, plasma erythropoietin rises within the first day or two. The new red cells arrive later. Why does the cell count lag the hormone?
scenes.caption: In lowlanders breathing thin air, plasma erythropoietin rises within the first day or two. The new red cells arrive later. Why does the cell count lag the hormone?
scenes.visual: Pull back to the full world. A day counter appears at the top, ticking 'day 1', 'day 2'. Two tracks are drawn at the right of frame, both unnumbered and tagged 'schematic': an upper MAGENTA track, 'EPO in plasma', which rises steeply over the first two ticks and then eases down while staying above its own starting level; and a lower RED track, 'new red cells', which stays flat and empty. MAGENTA dots stream from the kidney patch to the marrow block, and the marrow brightens but releases nothing yet. On the question, white text across the top: 'Why does the count lag?'

Predict pause. The question card stays. Near-stillness by design: the day counter holds, the MAGENTA track holds its shape, the RED track stays flat, the marrow block glows and pulses faintly, and red cells drift slowly along the vessel band. No other change.

scenes.tts: Erythropoietin acts mainly by preventing the death of late red cell progenitors. Those cells still have to divide and mature. Release of reticulocytes, young red cells that still hold RNA, rises over the following days.
scenes.narration: Erythropoietin acts mainly by preventing the death of late red cell progenitors. Those cells still have to divide and mature. Release of reticulocytes, young red cells that still hold RNA, rises over the following days.
scenes.caption: Erythropoietin acts mainly by preventing the death of late red cell progenitors. Those cells still have to divide and mature. Release of reticulocytes, young red cells that still hold RNA, rises over the following days.
scenes.visual: Question card dissolves. The camera pushes in on the TAN marrow block, which opens to show four round progenitor cells. Before the hormone arrives, two of them begin to crumble and fade; as MAGENTA dots land on newly arriving progenitors, the crumbling stops and all four survive intact. On 'divide and mature', each surviving cell splits once and its daughters shrink and smooth into RED discs carrying a faint speckled interior, one labelled 'reticulocyte (holds RNA)'. They move out through the marrow opening into the vessel band and join the drift. The day counter runs on through 'day 3' and 'day 4' while the lower RED track at the right now climbs gradually, lagging well behind the MAGENTA track's peak.

scenes.tts: So two unrelated events can move the same number, and the body is not aiming at that number. A kidney cell orders red cells for the tissue it can feel, and the ratio follows.
scenes.narration: So two unrelated events can move the same number, and the body is not aiming at that number. A kidney cell orders red cells for the tissue it can feel, and the ratio follows.
scenes.caption: So two unrelated events can move the same number, and the body is not aiming at that number. A kidney cell orders red cells for the tissue it can feel, and the ratio follows.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the full world, everything still moving. On 'two unrelated events', the tube runs its two changes again quickly as ghosts: the AMBER column swelling (marker down) and the AMBER column shrinking (marker up), with the RED column held still in both. On 'not aiming at that number', the WHITE marker and read-out dim again and the struck-through dial from s03 flashes once. On 'orders red cells for the tissue it can feel', the CYAN halo returns tight around the two interstitial cells, the MAGENTA arrow runs kidney to marrow again, and fresh RED discs leave the marrow into the vessel band. On 'the ratio follows', the RED column in the tube rises a short step LAST, after the cells have moved, and the marker edges up with it.

End card over the dimmed but still moving world (red cells drifting along the vessel band, the CYAN gauges glowing, MAGENTA dots crossing from kidney to marrow). Large centred white text: 'Hematocrit is a ratio; the kidney regulates its numerator by local oxygen.' The tube's RED column and the two interstitial cells pulse once in order behind the line.
